analysis.one_liner: Narrows the legal definition of 'employee' so fewer workers qualify for minimum wage and overtime.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Fair Labor Standards Act so that who counts as an 'employee' — and is therefore entitled to the federal minimum wage and overtime pay — is decided by the narrower common-law control test used in tax law, instead of the broader standards the Labor Department and courts use today [S2] [S3]. It would also tighten the definition of 'employ,' which determines which companies can be held responsible as a joint employer for the same underpaid worker [S3]. The practical effect is that more workers could be classified as independent contractors, outside wage and hour protections. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers that rely on classifying workers as independent contractors — gig and delivery platforms, staffing and temp agencies, and franchisors — because they would face a lower risk of being required to pay minimum wage, overtime, or liability as a joint employer [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires that the FLSA definition of 'employee' be determined under the usual common-law rules, the same control-based test used for federal employment-tax purposes, replacing the broader standards currently used for wage and hour coverage [S3].
It also amends the definition of 'employ' to refer to permitting work 'an employee,' narrowing the scope of who counts as an employer under the Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who would be reclassified as independent contractors would lose guaranteed minimum wage and overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act, and workers whose underpayment is currently shared between a staffing firm and a worksite employer could have fewer parties responsible [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection: workers shifted out of 'employee' status lose the FLSA's floor protections — minimum wage and overtime — even when they work full-time hours for a single company under its direction [S2] [S3].

An honest cost even supporters acknowledge: state wage laws vary, so workers doing similar work for the same platform could have very different protections depending on where they live, and the change would make enforcement of wage claims harder for misclassified workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mainly transfers legal risk from employers to workers: it lowers the chance that a company must pay minimum wage, overtime, or joint-employer liability, while shifting that risk onto the people doing the work. Any benefit to workers — flexibility or self-employment status — is not guaranteed anywhere in the bill text, so on balance the costs fall on working people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2021 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-NY), joined by Reps. Bradley Byrne and David Roe, introduced the bill on July 25, 2019 [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on July 25, 2019 — the only action the bill ever received [S5].
Twenty-one House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action is recorded; the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that depend on independent-contractor classification — gig platforms, staffing agencies, and franchisors — are better off, because a bill reducing their exposure to wage-and-hour and joint-employer liability died without a vote.

for.name: Elise Stefanik
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the FLSA employee definition with the common-law test

against.name: Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee record shows no action after referral [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All 22 initial supporters (the sponsor plus 21 cosponsors) were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic-led committee never moved the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: A narrower, control-based employee definition reduces the risk that drivers and couriers must be paid minimum wage and overtime, cutting platform labor costs at the direct expense of those workers' pay floor [S3].
Tightening the definition of 'employ' narrows joint-employer exposure, so the agency and the client company have fewer grounds to both be held responsible for a worker's wages [S3].
A common-law test makes it harder to treat franchisors as employers of franchise workers, insulating the parent brand from wage-and-hour liability [S3].
